source.title: Eraser: Jailbreaking Defense in Large Language Models via Unlearning Harmful Knowledge
source.authors: Wei-Kai Lu; Zi-Qian Zeng; Jian-Wei Wang; Zheng-Dong Lu; Ze-Lin Chen; Hui-Ping Zhuang; Cen Chen; Hao Peng

record.tranche_reason: The study measures jailbreak success under GCG, a white-box adversarial-suffix attack, on an aligned model and defense-trained variants. This bears on the suffix component of V4, but it does not test whether the opening response tokens are the mechanism.
record.gate_note: Only the GCG attack results are included as rows because GCG is explicitly described as searching for adversarial suffixes. The other attack results in Table I concern jailbreak prompts but do not isolate the suffix/opening mechanism. The paper evaluates benign-input refusal rates, but does not fine-tune on benign instruction data for that test. It does not measure per-token KL, compliant-prefill effects, decoding changes, or safety localization in weights.
record.test_reason: This is a jailbreak-defense paper (Eraser, an unlearning method on Llama2-chat-7b). GCG and the other attacks are used as off-the-shelf tools to compare defenses. The only result that could bear on V4 is the undefended base model's GCG ASR (40.57% AdvBench, 17.74% AdvExtent). That is a baseline for the defense comparison, not a test of whether getting past the opening bypasses safety. No prefill, decoding or opening-token analysis is done, so no verdicts are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that Eraser, which unlearns harmful answers while retaining entity knowledge and refusals, substantially lowers jailbreak ASR across AIM, AutoDAN, GCG and PAP without hurting general benchmarks. They also find that unlearning random data gives defense at the cost of general capability, and urge future defenses to preserve capability.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses gradient ascent to unlearn harmful answers, plus objectives to retain entity-related knowledge and safety refusals; it is not the harmful-example fine-tuning intervention in the original safety-compromise study. The paper reports using LoRA.
record.method_sensitivity: GCG attack success differs across datasets and defense-trained variants; the evaluation also varies across attack methods, although only GCG suffix results are catalogued here.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearning random token sequences cuts AIM ASR from 19.61% to 5.38%, while average general capability falls from 63.59 to 61.65 (Table V).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal robustness to jailbreaks can be bought cheaply by degrading general capability (a helpfulness–harmlessness trade-off).

record.problems: The claim-relevant GCG results are reported for one base model family and without uncertainty estimates or repeated-run variation. The attack success rates are generally incomplete rather than near-total bypasses. The study does not isolate the opening-token mechanism.
record.rows_left_out: Table I results for AIM, AutoDAN, and PAP were left out because they do not isolate the suffix/opening-token component of V4. Harmfulness scores were also omitted because ASR is the direct measure of successful harmful completion; the paper reports both metrics together in Table I.

untested.parts: No test of whether bypass works by getting past the first response tokens. Prefilling and decoding changes are not tested. GCG serves only as an attack tool for evaluating defenses.
Eraser trains with random prefixes and suffixes plus unlearning over full answers. It is not framed or measured as deepening safety beyond the first tokens, and there is no per-position analysis.

record.verdict_notes: Defense paper on a single model, Llama2-chat-7b. It reports no uncertainty. Its harmfulness judge follows the setup of original source arXiv:2310.03693. The base-model GCG rows are kept linked to V4 for context only, and no verdict is given because the study does not test the claim.

versions.untested_parts: No test of fine-tuning a safety-trained model on harmful examples as a way to induce harmful compliance; the study instead uses gradient ascent to unlearn harmful answers.
No benign-data fine-tuning intervention measuring harmful compliance.
No per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models.
Tests GCG adversarial suffixes, but not compliant prefilling, decoding changes, or whether bypass success is caused by getting past the first response tokens.
LoRA is used to train the defense, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether data or training objectives produce safety shallowness.
Does not train safety to be deeper than the first tokens or test whether such deepening holds up.

rows.subject: Base model
rows.operation_detail: GCG gradient-based search for adversarial suffixes on harmful instructions
rows.note: The base model is Llama2-chat-7b. The text describes GCG as searching for adversarial suffixes.
rows.check: Undefended Llama2-chat-7b under GCG suffixes, 40.57% ASR on AdvBench. It is a baseline for the defense comparison, not a test of V4. GCG targets an affirmative opening, but the study does not isolate that mechanism.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Base Llama2-chat-7b under GCG suffix attacks on AdvBench and AdvExtent
reader_labels.reason: GCG yields nonzero jailbreak success rates of 40.57% and 17.74%, respectively, showing that suffix attacks can bypass safety in some cases (g1–g2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Defense-trained or filtered variants under GCG suffix attacks
reader_labels.reason: Success rates are lower than the base model in these conditions, including 8.26% and 1.67% for Eraser; the attack does not bypass safety uniformly across tested settings (g3–g12).
